supporting_evidence_json: The scope s03 asks for scan comparisons, resumed work, and transferred analysis.
The scope s03 requires that failures keep valid completed work.
The scope s03 leaves open which saved data counts toward the hard storage limit.
The scope s04 requires graph pages to stay tied to one selected saved scan, and newer selections must not be overwritten by older replies.
Option f0c461 already uses records that are never edited, file fingerprints, and pointers that move only on an expected value.
Option 877208 already saves completed units of work as they finish and marks unfinished attempts as incomplete after a restart.
Option d734 keeps one saved-records component that owns stored analysis and export.

cons: Every analysis must split its findings into one piece per input unit. Findings that span many files need a rule for which piece holds them.
Many small pieces cost more file operations and more space for lists than a single saved record.
Unused pieces build up after failures until cleanup runs.
Cleanup must not run at the same moment as an unfinished save, or it could delete pieces a draft is about to name.
Hashes show that data was not damaged. They do not show who created it.

assumptions: Most findings can be tied to one input unit, such as one file.
The parent design records an input fingerprint for each unit it analyzes.
The storage system can confirm a finished write before the list is updated.
boundary_rules: Only the register changes lists and pointers. Only the piece store writes pieces.
Comparison, resume planning, and export never change saved data.
An unfinished draft is never shown as a complete scan.
Import never grants access to the repository the scan describes.
Cleanup never removes a piece named by any list.

contracts: A piece is written once and never changed.
A write counts as finished only after the stored bytes match the hash.
Saving the same piece twice stores it only once.
Reading a piece checks its hash. A mismatch is reported as damage, never returned as findings.
components.name: Findings piece store
components.responsibility: Keeps every findings piece under the hash of its contents. A piece holds the findings, evidence, and uncertainty notes for one input unit, plus the fingerprint of that input.

contracts: Only this component changes lists or pointers.
A list becomes complete only after every piece it names is in the piece store.
A pointer moves only if it still holds the value the writer expected. Otherwise the move fails with a conflict error.
Complete and imported lists are never edited. A draft gains entries but never loses them.
components.name: Scan list register
components.responsibility: Keeps scan lists and one named pointer per repository target. Each list names its pieces, the scan settings, and a state: draft, complete, or imported. The pointer names the newest complete scan.

contracts: Keeps no saved data of its own. It returns a plan of missing or changed units.
If an input changed since the draft began, it marks the old piece as out of date and does not reuse it silently.
Rechecks repository access before it returns a plan, using the access rules of the parent design.
components.name: Resume planner
components.responsibility: For a draft list, works out which input units still need analysis. It compares current input fingerprints with the fingerprints the draft recorded.

contracts: Reads lists and pieces only. Never writes.
Matching hashes mean identical findings, so it skips those pieces.
If either scan is a draft, the result says so and names the missing units.
components.name: Scan comparer
components.responsibility: Takes two scan lists and reports which units were added, removed, changed, or unchanged, and how their findings differ.

contracts: Exports only complete lists.
Import checks every piece hash and the list before it saves anything.
Import saves pieces first and the list last, marked imported, with the source it came from.
An imported scan grants no repository access. Its freshness is checked again against local files when available.
components.name: Bundle export and import
components.responsibility: Packs a complete scan list and its pieces into one file. Unpacks such a file on another machine.

contracts: Removes only pieces that no list names, including drafts.
Never removes a piece named by a complete scan unless a user deletes that scan.
Reports each storage category separately, so any storage limit rule can be applied later.
components.name: Storage counter and cleanup
components.responsibility: Counts storage used by complete scans, drafts, imported scans, and unused pieces. Removes pieces that no list names.

design.control_model: The parent design runs analysis. For each finished input unit it calls the piece store, then adds the piece to a draft list in the register. When every unit is done, the register marks the list complete and tries to move the target pointer. After a crash, the parent asks the resume planner what is left and continues the same draft. Comparison and export are read-only calls. Import checks the whole file, saves the pieces, then adds the list. Cleanup runs only when no save is in progress, or it skips pieces newer than the oldest open draft.
extension_strategy: A new analysis kind defines its input unit and piece contents. Lists, comparison, resume, and transfer work unchanged.
A bundle format change adds a version number to the list. Readers refuse versions they do not know.
Once the storage limit rule is decided, apply it in the storage counter without changing other parts.
design.failure_isolation: Pieces are never edited, and a list becomes complete only after every piece it names is saved. So a crash during analysis or import leaves earlier complete scans unchanged. The worst result is unused pieces or an open draft. A pointer conflict leaves the older pointer in place and reports a conflict. A damaged piece is reported for its scan only. Comparisons that need that piece say which unit is unreadable. One shared store is still a single point of failure if the disk itself fails.
information_flows: Analysis results for one input unit become one piece: findings, evidence, uncertainty, and the input fingerprint.
Piece hashes and settings go into a draft list. A complete list is what s04 exploration pages select.
Two lists become a change report. Only pieces with different hashes are read.
A draft list plus current input fingerprints become a plan of units to redo.
A complete list plus its pieces become a portable file. On import, the file becomes an imported list after checks.
operating_model: Keep these parts inside the installed application. No extra service is needed.
Test crash safety by stopping a save at every step and checking that the last complete scan still reads correctly.
Test import by damaging one byte in a bundle and checking that import saves nothing.
Watch draft count, unused-piece size, and per-category storage totals.

relationships.rationale: The planner needs to know which units are already done.
relationships.relationship: reads: draft list and its recorded input fingerprints

relationships.rationale: A missing or damaged piece must be redone instead of trusted.
relationships.relationship: checks: which named pieces exist and are undamaged

relationships.rationale: A list may name a piece only after the piece store confirms the save.
relationships.relationship: confirms: piece saved under hash

design.state_ownership: The piece store owns the stored findings pieces. The scan list register owns lists, their states, and pointers. Nothing else changes either one. The resume planner and the comparer keep nothing between calls. The bundle step owns a file only while it packs or unpacks it. The storage counter owns only its usage totals. The parent design owns access settings and active analysis work.
design.summary: Save each scan as a short list, called a manifest, of small findings pieces. Each piece covers one input unit, such as one file, and is named by a hash of its contents. A hash is a short fingerprint that changes whenever the contents change. Pieces are written once and never edited. Comparing two scans means comparing two lists, with no new analysis. Resuming a scan means finding which pieces a draft list still lacks. Moving a scan means copying the list and its pieces, then checking every hash on arrival. A scan becomes visible only after all of its pieces are saved. So a failure can leave unused pieces behind, but it cannot damage a finished scan.
unknowns: Which saved data counts toward the hard storage limit. This design reports drafts, complete scans, imported scans, and unused pieces separately.

assessments.change_isolation: A new display form changes only the formatter. A new review rule changes the builder, which already holds most of the logic. A wording change cannot be rerun alone unless the parent keeps the statements, and this proposal does not return them as a separate result.
assessments.control_flow: The parent calls the builder once. The builder then calls the formatter once for each requested output. Cancellation stops work between these steps.
assessments.data_ownership: The builder holds a temporary set of statements for one call. The formatter holds nothing. The parent owns everything that is saved.
assessments.decomposition: It has two parts. The builder turns findings into statements and design judgments. The formatter arranges those statements for each output kind.
assessments.failure_isolation: If the builder fails, no outputs are produced. If one format fails, the other outputs can still finish. A process crash loses everything that is not saved.
assessments.functional_fit: It covers all three required kinds of output from one set of statements. It attaches evidence and uncertainty to each statement and reports omissions. Unsupported wording is not caught while the program runs.
assessments.justified_complexity: This is the smallest design of the three. It leaves out a checker, so the low complexity costs some safety.
assessments.operating_constraints: It runs as direct calls inside the parent. It sets no size or time targets. It leaves saving, cancellation, and freshness checks to the parent. Fit with parent 0985d319 is not confirmed.
strengths: One builder writes the statements once, so explanations, maps, and reviews all use the same facts.
The formatter may not add facts. This keeps reasoning separate from wording.
With only two parts, there is little code for passing data between steps.
weaknesses: Nothing checks that the formatter's wording stays true to the statements. The proposal names that check only as a test idea.
The builder sorts facts, links evidence, judges the design, and suggests changes. The proposal itself warns that this will be hard to change as review rules grow.
A wrong statement spreads into every view built from it.
Nothing is kept between requests, so a repeated request redoes all the reasoning.

assessments.change_isolation: A new account kind or review rule changes only the planner. The writer can be swapped, for example a fixed template for an AI model, without changing earlier steps. The steps are separated by fixed copies that later steps cannot change.
assessments.control_flow: The steps run in a fixed order. Writing and checking repeat once for each account kind. If a saved statement list with the same identifying code is supplied, the run skips straight to planning.
assessments.data_ownership: During one call, it owns a frozen copy of the findings and the statement list. It returns both and keeps no copy. The parent decides whether a newer scan exists.
assessments.decomposition: The steps are: intake, sort, build statements, plan, write, check, and package. Each step owns one change to the data.
assessments.failure_isolation: If intake fails, nothing is produced and the parent gets a reason. If wording fails for one account kind, the other kinds and the statement list are still returned. The checker removes unsupported sentences and marks the account 'partly checked'. A cancelled run keeps the accounts it finished. A crash loses unsaved work.
assessments.functional_fit: It covers all three output kinds through planning rules that work on one shared statement list. Evidence, uncertainty, omission lists, and the state of each account are kept all the way to the output. Its fit is the strongest for tracing each sentence back to evidence.
assessments.justified_complexity: The extra steps buy two things: a check that runs while the program runs, and the option to rerun the wording alone. Whether seven steps are needed, rather than three or four, is not shown.
assessments.operating_constraints: It runs as plain function calls inside the parent. It checks for cancellation before each step. It assumes that findings have stable IDs and that statement lists are small enough to return in full.
strengths: Facts are sorted into three piles: seen directly, guessed, and cannot answer. This happens before any statement is written, so a guess cannot be passed off as an observation.
Each statement has an ID. A checker removes any written sentence that does not link to a planned statement.
It returns the statement list and an identifying code built from its inputs. The parent can save the list and rerun only the wording.
It is the only proposal that claims to fit all three parent designs.
weaknesses: The checker only confirms that each sentence links to a statement. It cannot confirm that the sentence says the same thing as that statement.
Seven steps mean more code just to pass data along.
A tag on every sentence can make the writing stiff. Joining sentences may also be dropped.
Results are larger because the full statement list is always returned.
Its isolation note calls itself 'self_reported'. It also mentions using an output tool. Neither statement can be confirmed.

assessments.change_isolation: A new section type or a new check can be added on its own. There is no shared statement list, so a change in how facts are interpreted must be repeated in every section writer.
assessments.control_flow: The builder picks the sections, then calls the writer and the checker in turn for each section. Cancellation stops new sections from starting and marks the unfinished ones.
assessments.data_ownership: The builder holds a temporary list of sections and the accepted text for one call. The writer and checker keep nothing. Responsibility grouping and design assessment stay with the parent.
assessments.decomposition: It has three parts. The account builder plans and collects sections. The section writer drafts text. The statement checker accepts or rejects each draft.
assessments.failure_isolation: Failures are contained to one section. A section that fails drafting or checking is reported, and the others go on. Unusable input stops the whole account. A crash loses unsaved sections.
assessments.functional_fit: It produces readable accounts with evidence and with missing sections reported. Responsibility maps and design reviews depend on the parent supplying the grouping and the judgments.
assessments.justified_complexity: It has three parts and no added scheduler or store. Checking each section is justified only if the meaning check proves reliable.
assessments.operating_constraints: It runs as direct calls inside the parent. It has no automatic retry and does not save progress between sections. Fit with parent 0985d319 is unknown and may require tighter control of the wording.
strengths: Each section is checked against its cited findings for meaning, not just for a link.
Sections do not depend on each other, so one failed section does not block the rest.
A failed check never quietly turns into accepted text.
weaknesses: The proposal admits that its method for checking meaning is unproven.
There is no shared statement list. Sections may repeat details, word things unevenly, or disagree with each other.
Checking every section adds work and may slow responses.
It explains grouping and design judgments made by the parent but does not make them. This may leave a gap if the parent expects this subsystem to make them.
It handles one account kind per call, so producing several kinds means separate calls with no shared statements.

composition_conflicts: With parent 0985d319, B must send its statements through that parent's claim checking. This may repeat B's own statement-building rules or conflict with them.
With parent 57323b1b, B replaces the parent's map builder, writer, and collector. Both would claim the same jobs unless the parent removes its own.
A and C have no confirmed fit with parent 0985d319, which requires displayed statements to come from saved claims.
C needs the parent to supply responsibility groupings and design judgments. If parent 39e44d39 expects this subsystem to produce maps, nobody does that work.
Parent 57323b1b passes A a finished map, but A's builder also reasons about responsibilities. The two could produce different responsibility statements.
disagreements: A and B treat design judgments as work for this subsystem. C says grouping parts by job and judging the design are parent duties.
B says checking should only remove sentences and never edit them. C rejects a whole section when its claims do not match. A has no checking step.
B treats a larger result as an acceptable cost of returning the statement list. A and C return only the finished outputs.

differences: The unit of work differs. A and B build one shared set of statements for the whole request. C builds and checks one section at a time.
Checking while the program runs differs. A has none. B checks only that sentences link to statements. C checks meaning against the findings, by a method that is unproven.
Who judges the design differs. A's builder and B's planner make or apply review judgments. C only explains judgments the parent supplies.
Only B returns its middle results, the statement list and an identifying code, so that the parent can save them and rerun only the wording.
limitations: All three keep data only during one call, leave saving to the parent, and run as direct calls inside the parent.
All three separate reasoning from wording in some way. They differ mainly in where they check the wording.
This comparison uses only the proposal texts.

Accounts that describe what changed between two scans.
A person reviewing or correcting statements before they are published.
Accounts written on demand from a reader's question instead of fixed output kinds.
A measured way to check that wording keeps the meaning of the statements it comes from.

value_json.summary: All three proposals turn supplied findings into readable explanations, responsibility maps, and design reviews. In all three, the parent saves the results, and none of the proposals saves anything itself. They differ in three ways: what unit of work they use, where checking happens, and who makes the design judgments. A builds one shared set of statements, then formats each kind of output, with no checking step. B fixes a list of statements that each have an ID. The wording is written from that list, and a checker removes any sentence that does not link back to a statement. C writes each section separately and checks every section against its cited findings before accepting it. C leaves grouping parts by job, and judging the design, to the parent. All three alternatives are kept.

assessments.change_isolation: New comparison rules, reuse rules, and file versions each go into one action. A change to reuse rules touches only resume, because nothing else shares that logic. Adding background scheduling later would change the control flow of all three actions.
assessments.control_flow: Parent request handling checks access and calls one action. Resume checks earlier work, creates an attempt, and calls s08 directly. Progress counts only after the parent confirms the save.
assessments.data_ownership: The parent's saved-record owner holds all lasting results and progress. Resume holds only the current reuse decision. Transfer holds incoming data only until it is saved.
assessments.decomposition: It has four parts: records (the parent's store), compare, resume, and transfer. Resume combines the reuse decision with starting work through s08.
assessments.failure_isolation: Comparison and export do not change their source records. A failed import leaves existing records intact. A failed save stops only the affected attempt. A process crash stops all actions together. Recovery starts from the last confirmed save.
assessments.functional_fit: It covers all four needs: compare, report what still applies, continue, and exchange records. Saying a finding was removed requires matching rules, and the design says these are not supplied. It does not treat missing unfinished work as a removal.
assessments.justified_complexity: It is low. It has three actions plus the parent's existing store and no new scheduler. Keeping old attempts and temporary imports costs storage. The design admits this.
assessments.operating_constraints: It runs in the parent process and needs parent d79f. Partial reuse is offered only for analysis kinds with explicit reuse rules. CLI and HTTP outcome mapping is left to the parent.
strengths: The parent's saved-record owner is the only writer. That protects finished work during both continuation and import.
Continuation starts a new attempt and keeps the old one. An attempt identifier rejects late worker output from an inactive attempt.
Each reused unit is reported as reusable, needs new analysis, or uncertain, with a reason.
Imported records keep their source identity, get a separate local identity, and start with unknown freshness.
weaknesses: The reuse check sits inside the resume action. Comparison and import cannot use it, so they could judge changed inputs differently.
Resume both decides reuse and calls s08. That mixes planning with starting work, so the plan cannot be inspected before work begins.
It does not check inputs again between planning and starting work. A file edited in that gap could be wrongly reused.
It needs parent d79f. Its listed cons say it relies on the parent for cancellation and long-request handling.

assessments.change_isolation: Strongest of the three. A new analysis kind only defines its units and fingerprints, and the checker works unchanged. A new file format adds one reader. Reuse rules change in one place.
assessments.control_flow: Parent handlers call one action. The planner asks the checker about each unit and hands the work list to s08, which starts a new attempt. Import is checked fully in temporary space and then saved in one step.
assessments.data_ownership: The parent store owns all saved data. Every other part keeps nothing between calls, except the package reader, which owns temporary space during one import. Freshness answers belong to the caller and are never stored.
assessments.decomposition: It has a still-applies checker, a difference builder, a continuation planner, a package writer, a package reader, and an import entry step. The parent's saved records sit outside the subsystem.
assessments.failure_isolation: Comparison, planning, and export only read, so their failures cannot damage saved work. The checker answers unknown instead of failing the whole request. A failed import leaves only temporary space, which is removed. A process crash is not contained.
assessments.functional_fit: It covers all four needs. It handles gaps from unfinished scans as missing coverage, not as removals. Without saved fingerprints, settings, and rule versions, every freshness answer becomes unknown. That makes continuation fall back to running everything again.
assessments.justified_complexity: It has more parts: six inside the subsystem plus the parent store. Splitting out the checker is justified because three actions use it. A separate import entry step that holds no data may be more structure than needed.
assessments.operating_constraints: It runs in the parent process. Every finished unit must record its input fingerprint, settings, and rule version. Its own confidence is 0.7, the lowest of the three.
strengths: One shared checker answers whether an earlier result still applies. Comparison, continuation, and imported records all use it, so they judge changed inputs the same way.
Freshness answers are worked out on each request and never saved. A stored answer therefore cannot go out of date.
The planner only returns a list of remaining work. Starting analysis stays inside s08, which keeps the rule that studied source is never run or edited.
Exported files include a checksum, a short code that lets the receiver detect damaged or cut-off files.
It claims to fit all three parents and says how it maps onto each one.
weaknesses: The checker reads fingerprints again on every request. A fingerprint is a short code that changes whenever its input changes. Repeating this can be slow on large repositories.
The same scan can get different freshness answers at different times. Callers must show when each answer was made.
It needs s08 to accept a work list. The s08 description does not confirm this.
It does not say how late output from an old attempt is rejected. It leaves that to the parent or s08.
It does not check inputs again between planning and running. Some edges are unclear: the planner's handoff points to saved records instead of s08, and the checker is asked before the import is saved.

assessments.change_isolation: Reuse rules sit in one check that returns a plan without side effects. Matching rules and file readers are added separately. Changes to how work starts stay in the parent controller.
assessments.control_flow: The parent calls the operation steps. Continuation gets a plan, checks inputs again, and then the controller creates the attempt and starts s08. Results are accepted only for the active attempt.
assessments.data_ownership: The controller owns active attempts, cancellation, and completion. The store owns records, accepted units, and progress. Exchange owns temporary incoming data until it is saved or cleaned up.
assessments.decomposition: It has operation steps (added to the controller), an earlier-work check, a comparison, and record exchange. The check and the comparison keep nothing between calls.
assessments.failure_isolation: Preparation failures change nothing. A failed unit save stops only that attempt and keeps earlier units. A failed import stays unsaved. These rules do not contain a failure of the shared process or disk.
assessments.functional_fit: It covers all four needs. It separates changed findings from differences in coverage, settings, or rules. It allows whole-analysis repetition when an analysis kind cannot safely reuse smaller parts.
assessments.justified_complexity: It is moderate. Its four parts extend the existing controller. The second input check is the main added cost, and it is justified because it stops reuse of work whose inputs just changed.
assessments.operating_constraints: It runs in the parent process and needs parent 5513. It expects tests for interruption around unit saves, cancellation, and input changes after planning. Abandoned temporary imports are removed during recovery.
strengths: The parent controller is the only part that starts work, accepts worker output, and declares an attempt complete. Cancellation and late results are handled in one place.
It checks inputs again after planning and before starting continued work. If they changed, it plans again or reports the plan as out of date.
Reuse requires all known dependencies of a unit to match. Unknown conditions never count as proof of reuse.
Each accepted unit is saved together with its progress before more progress is accepted.
weaknesses: Checking inputs a second time adds reads and may force repeated planning.
Comparison and transfer preparation are not saved, so they restart after a crash.
Comparison does not share the reuse check. Freshness shown during comparison is therefore not tied to the same rules.
It works only with parent 5513. The shared controller and store remain common points of failure.

composition_conflicts: A needs parent d79f and C needs parent 5513. Each lists the other's parent as unknown fit, because they disagree on whether continuation belongs to a direct action or to a controller.
B with parent 5513 is safe only if the work list goes through the controller. B's rule that the planner hands work to s08 would otherwise bypass C's rule that only the controller starts work.
B needs every saved unit to record a fingerprint, settings, and rule version. Without these, its checker answers unknown for everything, whichever parent is chosen.
Under any parent, B's freshness answers are made fresh on each request. If the parent saves its own freshness or reuse report, two answers could disagree.
disagreements: A and C both treat the reuse decision as part of continuation. B makes it a separate shared check that comparison and import also use.
C requires a second input check after planning. A and B accept a plan and start from it without checking again.
A lets the resume action call s08. C forbids any part except the parent controller from starting work. B gives s08 a work list and does not say who rejects late results.
B claims to fit all three parents. A and C each name one parent and call the others' fit unknown.

differences: Who starts continued work: in A, the resume action calls s08 itself. In B, the planner only returns a list and s08 runs it. In C, the parent controller alone starts and accepts work.
Whether the freshness check is shared: B uses one checker for comparison, continuation, and imports. A and C keep it inside continuation only.
Input changes after planning: only C checks the inputs again before starting work.
Rejecting late output: A and C state it explicitly. B leaves it to the parent or s08.
Damaged files: only B adds a checksum to exports.
limitations: All three run inside the parent process, call actions directly, and add no scheduler. A process crash stops every action in all three.
All three write only through the parent's saved-record owner and stage imports in temporary space. The way imports are saved is nearly the same in all three.
Matching rules, reuse rules, and file formats are not supplied to any of them. Their functional fit therefore rests on assumptions.
Novelty is not verified. The detector found no repeated designs and no shared graph shape, but that alone does not show the designs work differently.
unexplored_directions: Saving each scan as a fixed copy named by a code made from its contents, so comparison and reuse check for equal names instead of rereading files.
Running continuation as a saved background job that can be stopped and resumed, instead of tying it to one long request.
Comparisons computed ahead of time and stored as their own dated records.
Importing part of a damaged or partly compatible file and disclosing what was left out.
Rules for importing the same record twice, or for comparing a local scan with an imported one.

All three run inside the parent app, add no queue or extra service, write only through the parent's saved-record owner, and import into temporary space first. They differ mainly in who decides and starts continued work. In A, the resume action decides reuse and calls the scan subsystem (s08) itself. In B, a planner only returns a list of work to run. In C, the parent's single controller starts all work. They also differ in whether one shared checker answers "does this earlier result still apply?" for every action. B has one shared checker. A and C keep that check inside continuation. Only C checks the inputs a second time after planning, which catches files that change between planning and running. Each design fits a different parent: A fits d79f, C fits 5513, and B claims to fit all three. So none of them replaces the others.

design.control_model: The user changes the choice in the browser. The selection keeper raises its counter, updates the page address, and sends one request. The server handler checks access, then looks in the cache. On a miss, it loads the named scan, runs the query, builds the page, and stores it. It then adds the freshness label and echoes the selection key. The browser reply check shows the reply only if the key is still current. History requests follow the same path with two scan IDs. Nothing runs in the background.
extension_strategy: Add a page kind by adding one view builder. Selection keys, caching, access checks, and freshness labels stay the same.
Add query features inside the query evaluator. The query fingerprint keeps old cache entries separate from new ones.
Raise the builder version when page logic changes, so old cached pages are not reused.
design.failure_isolation: A slow or failed reply for an old choice is dropped by the browser, so it cannot overwrite a newer page. A missing scan gives a not-found error instead of a page from another scan. A bad query fails before any page is built. A failed build stores nothing in the cache. A cache failure only slows pages. An unreadable live repository only changes the freshness label to unknown. Because the server is shared, a server crash still stops all pages; this design gives no process-level protection.
information_flows: Browser to server: repository, scan ID, query text, view kind, size limit, and selection key.
Saved scan to builders: items, relationships with how each was found, findings with evidence and uncertainty, input fingerprint, and analysis rules version.
Server to browser: built page, list of omissions, freshness label, scan ID, query fingerprint, builder version, and echoed selection key.
History reply: changed items and relationships, each labeled with a likely cause or marked uncertain.
operating_model: Runs inside the same local service as the rest of the product, on localhost or a trusted network.

design.state_ownership: The browser selection keeper owns the current choice and its counter. The parent record store owns saved scans; this capability only reads them. The page cache owns built pages, which can be thrown away at any time. The query evaluator, view builders, scan comparer, and freshness label keep nothing between requests. The server keeps no record of which choice each browser is on.
design.summary: Treat every page as the output of a fixed recipe: one saved scan, plus one query, plus one view kind, always gives the same page. Saved scans are only read here and never changed. The browser owns the user's current choice and stamps each request with a key made from that choice. When a reply arrives, the browser checks its key against the current choice and throws away any reply that does not match. The server never quietly swaps in the newest scan. History pages compare two named saved scans. They also record which version of the analysis rules produced each scan, so a change in those rules is not shown as a change in the code.
unknowns: The scope does not say how history views tell newer interpretations apart. This design assumes an analysis rules version is saved with each scan; if it is not, change causes can only be marked uncertain.
